query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, boron microalloying combined with controlled thermal processing creates a refined microstructure in which in situ precipitation of TiB2 particles and dynamic amorphization lead to a robust, passivating near-surface layer that simultaneously reduces wear-induced damage and retards corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloy coating with conventional coarse microstructure and no boron addition.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small amount of boron to the alloy composition and apply controlled thermal processing designed to trigger dynamic amorphization and in situ TiB2 formation in the near-surface region.
generation.conditions: Testing in a combined mechanical wear and corrosive environment (e.g., sliding wear under 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under controlled temperature conditions that allow the formation and stabilization of the desired microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined near-surface layer featuring nano-scale TiB2 precipitates embedded in a dynamically amorphized matrix.
generation.mechanism: Boron acts as a microalloying element that, during controlled thermal processing, promotes the formation of finely dispersed TiB2 particles. This refinement creates a dense, passivating surface structure that minimizes the nucleation of corrosion sites, while dynamic amorphization under mechanical stress continuously regenerates or maintains the integrity of the passivation, resulting in lower wear rates and enhanced corrosion resilience.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy without boron microalloying and thermal processing, the modified alloy will demonstrate significantly reduced wear rates, higher corrosion potentials, and lower corrosion current densities, indicating improved resistance to combined wear and corrosion degradation.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy that lacks boron microalloying and is processed without the controlled thermal treatment, which maintains a coarser microstructure and lacks the in situ formation of TiB2.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits are expected to hold under conditions where the thermal processing parameters are optimized to avoid excessive TiB2 growth (which could impair passivation) and in environments similar to those simulated (e.g., moderate temperature saline conditions). The hypothesis might fail under extreme conditions where the passive layer itself is unstable or in cases of over-doping with boron.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in wear and corrosion resistance are uncertain and will depend on optimal boron content and precise thermal processing conditions. The interplay of dynamic amorphization and passive film stability under varying service loads also requires further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based HEA coatings: one set incorporating boron microalloying with controlled thermal processing and a control set without boron and standard processing. Expose both sets to identical sliding wear and 3.5 wt.% NaCl corrosion conditions while monitoring their tribological and electrochemical responses.
measurements: Average wear rate (mm³/N-m) through direct measurement of material loss
Corrosion potential and current density via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and linear polarization measurements
Post-test microstructural analysis (SEM, EDS) to assess the formation and stability of the near-surface passivating layer and distribution of TiB2 particles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-enhanced, thermally processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both wear and corrosion metrics (i.e., no lower wear rate, unchanged or inferior corrosion potential/current, and no evidence of a refined, passivating surface microstructure) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study demonstrates that the proposed alloy design delivers substantial improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance. The work clarifies how boron doping modifies the microstructure, establishes the linkage between microstructural features and performance, and derives general design principles for engineering coatings. We define this strategy as a generalized methodology for coating performance enhancement. While the present study does not address specific service environments, machinability, or long-term stability, we contend that with its robust performance foundation, the coating can be further optimized through compositional tuning and post-processing to enable reliable service across a broad range of applications.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

reading.lever: Combine boron microalloying with controlled thermal processing to induce a refined, passivating near-surface layer via in situ TiB2 formation and dynamic amorphization.
reading.why: Prior evidence shows that microstructural refinement and in situ formation of protective phases are key to synergistic wear and corrosion resistance, addressing limitations in high-entropy alloy systems.
